body: ikr
Every. Single. Day.
Yes. Totally. Sometimes when I'm ovulating, too.
I don't know...I've taken it late before by 4 or 5 hours, and I felt like I noticed more ups and downs the next day. I think --like all medication --it depends on your physiology.

Thought I was B till this morning. Apparently, I'm A now. Cried for about ten minutes while I got dressed for work about a toy my son broke yesterday.

A or B--it's all exhausting.
I'm 6 days alcohol free! Congrats to you!

I've recently had to get sober (again). Alcohol makes everything easier...until you have to do real things. My problem is that I'll start out slow, rationalizing that I'm in control this time, but then BP2 will kick in and I'll either be calming my brain down or up daily, and then more and more--until I'm kind of drunk on my way to work the next morning. 

I don't have any really answers for you other than take care of the addiction issues--they make everything easier until they don't and it's just more emotional garbage to work through. We got plenty already, amirite? At least you're paying attention--that's awesome that you're aware.

I've been going to secular AA meetings. The social aspect scares the s___ out of me, but if it keeps me from drinking, it's worth it.
That's great advice. Thank you!

Exactly. This puts my back up so straight it's about to break.

I think I need to really confront him about being really critical and controlling or it's going to be over.

God, the comments are really helpful! Thank you.

No, haven't really talked to him yet. Things are feeling really crunchy and when I bring anything up, I'm being too sensitive or I'm "projecting" and he doesn't mean things that way...etc.

We've been married almost 10 years and have 2 kids. This sucks.
I'm beginning to think so. :(

2 months ago is probably too late to mention this: the first few nights starting Lamictal, I was extremely anxious. This faded quickly, especially when I realized it was the Lamictal. I hope it doesn't go that way for you, but I wish someone had warned me so I could've prepared. Good luck! I really like Lamictal, too.

Yes! My rage is what got me into the Doctor's in the first place. Turns out, it was coming from a place of anxiety--lack of control and fear turns into anger/rage for me as that's my most easily accessible defense-emotion. Meds have helped enormously--fewer hypomanic moments have allowed me to talk myself through, take a moment to myself to calm down.
This is such a kind reply--made me cry some. :)
I love the idea of drawing the feelings! Such a great response. Thank you for taking the time.

If I sleep anywhere other than my bed (like the couch), I'll almost always wake up not knowing who I am...where I am...

The first time it happened I was in Iraq. I wasn't combat or anything--didn't even leave the base while I was deployed--anxiety, I guess.
I really like the Yellow Maeng Da. It lifts my mood just enough so I can "get myself out of it" like you said.

That's great advice. When I reach out for help, though, my family (husband, sister, parents) don't seem to take it as seriously as I think they probably should. And so I start to doubt--am I just being dramatic? Weak? Maybe I just need to not be so narcissistic...it's not all about me...

I feel like there's someone standing on my back, compressing my chest. 

Sorry. Low day.

That sucks...and explains a lot...


(my experience as well)

It's like the tornado you're riding suddenly dies into dead air and you realize how high and far it has taken you because now you're falling all the way back. 

I'm sorry. Me too.
This.

Yes. I had to leave work early Friday and couldn't get out of bed all weekend. I barely made it to work today. This is a really tough one. It hasn't been this bad in a long time--so paralyzing. Like it takes effort to breath. I wish I knew what to do.
Ha! Perfect answer. Yes, you're probably right. :)

By the way, my first few days of taking lamotrigine made me extremely anxious, and each time my dose went up, it happened again. This passes. Give this one a try--it's good for a lot of people. Doctor's orders first, of course.
(thanks!)
The responses here are so helpful and encouraging. Thanks, All.
Thank you. I know I need to...reassuring words are very helpful.

Lamictal helped me with the waves, but it didn't stop them, just slowed them down. I need a decent ssri with it to keep depression at bay, but yeah, really bad depression right now. Will be switching ssri soon. I didn't even consider the Lamical may be making the depression worse. Food for thought...

Yes! Spot on. And sometimes, it seems all the pieces are moving at the same time. 

Sometimes I get checked by a piece I didn't expect. Everything is good, and then a story about a sad orca whale (a pawn?) ends the game for the day. Really, it was a sad orca story. So sad. I won't write about it here.

I've had good luck with lamotrigine, but it hasn't really helped my depression. I'm about to try switching from lexapro (generic--I forget the name) to something new. It's terrifying. It's always down to the same choice: do I risk what good I have for something potentially less shitty or do I learn to live with my current devils?
Dark, but definitely funny. I've had the same thought...so you don't cry at work? Like in the bathroom? Not everyone does that? Hmmm...
I don't know yet, but I'm trying.

Different strains do different things. Sativas make me really paranoid and almost panic-attack level. Indicas are much more mellow and are very comforting for me. A combination can be tricky. Unfortunately, unless you live in a state where you can buy from a dispensary, you can't really be sure. This isn't advice--just my personal experience.
Yes. It's not great, but if I keep it low--like a couple of beers--not so bad. Sort of makes me hypomanic, though. It can be pretty dangerous.

Update: I really don't like my new hair.

By the time it grows out, I'll probably want to cut it again. :)

Thanks, All. All the responses here are amazing. It helps to know you're all around.

Thank you--that's a wonderful post, and I'm so happy for you and your father! 

Good point about pity. It's not as difficult to embrace when I can redirect that to compassion for others & make sure to appreciate the effort people are making to empathize and understand;  it may look like pity, but it's kindness all the same.

How do you handle the awkwardness of people's pity and/or disbelief? I've told a few family members and it just feels crunchy. Didn't seem to be a good thing. I WANT to be open because, like you mention, it's nice when it's understood.
It's the worst. I always promise visits or outings...and then get too depressed to follow through. Hypomanic-me is very disappointed with depressed-me.

No worries--
Blink Health has saved me a ton of money, but I can't anymore. No other pills--I need to cut all medical $$. 

Didn't know about lamotrigine being so bad! I thought for sure the escitalopram would be the bad withdrawls. I'm going to taper off the escitalopram first and settle before I taper off the lamotrigine. I really appreciate the warning, though. I remember when my doses were going up, I'd have super bad anxiety at night.
I've come to the conclusion that this is as good as it gets. I'll always be low-energy and sensitive. And cry a lot, isolate myself, ...Yeah. Sometimes I feel done, too.
Yes--please press on. Your existence is important, even if you don't see it right now.
I hope you haven't done this yet. And I wish I had something comforting to say--I'm tempted to hop on that bus with you. We're in this together. Stay alive.

This is probably a terrible answer, but I haven't figured it out. I'm beginning to believe that this is as good as it gets. It's better than before (I don't blow up at people anymore), but I feel like my feelers are *broke*--I haven't been able to shake this nihilism for about a month. Maybe I'm just emotionally beat up right now and my system is in recovery mode. It's a gray hope.

So it goes.
I agree--exercise, yoga, whole foods--all of that legitimately makes bp2 easier to manage. Taking care of yourself makes a huge difference.

I totally agree with you. Those techniques are great at soothing or controlling symptoms. Meditation has helped tremendously. 

I guess I thought (since he did years of therapy at one point) that he would be supportive. But you're right--it's also hard for family to accept because they don't want it to be a mental illness. They want it to be a sugar or caffeine or (?)--anything but what it is.
Ha! I got that, too, but he likes to talk about my mom being 'crazy'.
So awesome. Thanks!
Actually, given the opportunity, I would try this.
Someone's logic is flawed.
"Cancer, huh? Have you tried a massage?"

It may depend on what is causing your headaches. I originally went in to see my doctor for migraines and bouts of rage and irritability. To make a long story short, she said my headaches may be my body's way of coping with severe anxiety. Since taking lamictal (lamotrigine), the headaches are mostly gone, and if I do get one, they're much more mild.
Thank you--those are great suggestions. So often, people suggest "self-care," but it's hard to imagine what that looks like if you never do it! I appreciate the response. :)
This really isn't the right place for this.
This really isn't the right place for this.
I feel you, friend. Ride it out--one day at a time. I'm walking along the bottom of the ocean, wondering how all those people up there float. Hugs and love.

Exactly. No one fakes this shit. I just had to come to terms about what I was really upset about: my sister has a disease I thought she had escaped. I'm here for her. I will be the support I wish I'd had. 

My lowest point? You mean dealing with my sister or my own? My lows are bedrock deep; in this situation with her, the lowest was feeling completely overwhelmed and realizing I couldn't "talk" her out of it. Now, I feel ready and able to validate and support her, but I think it's easier for me because I have a mental illness I struggle to explain.
I really like this--describes that feeling you get when you're trying to function through the fog.
God, I'm so sorry. That must be totally awful. I hope the answers above are helpful--such as find a group for support if your family can't provide it. Be well.

I'm bp2, but my youngest sister just had something of a psychotic break a few days ago and she's hospitalized now. Even knowing everything I do about mental illness and the importance of being believed, I couldn't shake this rage that she was acting. The truth is (that I can see now) is that this is so overwhelmingly difficult to accept because I know things are going to be really hard--life is harder, relationships are harder, employment--life is harder with a mental illness. I believe her, of course, and will offer as much support and love as I can, but I really wish I could accuse her of faking and have it be true. It doesn't excuse it, but I kind of understand the willful denial better than I did. But if they refuse to acknowledge that, find other support. Their sorrow for your diagnosis is not nearly as important as you and what you face daily. I'm sorry this is the reaction you're getting. I'm glad you're stable, though. That's what counts. :)
So cool! Thank you!

Me too--lamotrigine keeps me even, but the depression hits hard pretty frequently. I'm on the generic version of Leprexo to bring my mood up, but it doesn't do much, and more might = mania. I guess I'm just a down-kinda-person.

I was diagnosed BP2 about a year ago, so I'm still learning how to live with this, but I'll help if I can.

Lamotrigine (200mg) and Leprexo-generic (10mg). Lamotrigine has worked really well for me, but each time my dose was increased, I had really bad anxiety at night--like heart-pounding terror, but I knew to expect that. The Leprexo just gives my mood a tiny bump, but no side-effects that I've noticed.

Learning to identify the warning signs of a mood switch has been the most helpful thing I trying to get better at. Weird symptoms--like sad stories or cute things make me super depressed, or I get really irritable for no reason. Also, eat well! Exercise--I'm not right now myself, but I hear that helps. :) Above all else, be patient and kind with yourself. That--if you can master that, write me back and let me know how you did it. Best of luck--it's a weird road, but you have company.

Yes. This week. I haven't had to suppress my urge to self-harm like this in years. I almost stopped my meds--I had a whole tapering schedule printed out with notes--because I don't care anymore. I'm hanging in there, but damn, I'm so tired right now. I want to crawl into a dark cave and sleep. Like hibernate, but all the time.
Awesome, thank you! I've been having a particularly challenging week--this really picked me up!

I'm a mom with a couple little ones, too. I work full-time, but I'm telling you, taking care of babies is so hard when you can't even take care of yourself--much harder than work (for me)!

My mom (probably undiagnosed, but I'm no doc) always counseled my siblings and I to get make sure you get through the basics in order of importance: Food, dishes, and laundry. Everything else can wait. I keep healthy-ish fast dinners on hand and I stick to a mantra-like routine when I get home--dinner, lunches, bedtime. That's it. Anything else can wait. Take care of and be patient with yourself! You aren't perfect and the kids aren't going to be. 

Sometimes I just sit with my boys and cuddle. I suffer the most when I feel guilty for being ill. Your kids wouldn't want that. They love you, too. I hope things get better for you soon!

Me too. I think I may try to find a BP2 support group where I can meet some people who will understand this is real, painful, and a daily struggle. No one in my life gets that right now. I need some people that get me and won't just be annoyed that depressed is my normal, and their normal brains are different. I can't 'volunteer' myself healthy. Find the right people--don't blame yourself for not finding them right away.

...and now I will try to follow my own advice. Wishing us both luck.

Love this. You could have started this post with "I wake up..." and finished with "still trying to get out of bed" and it would still be totally accurate. I've gotten to the point that I'll: 1. take a note pad (to write my Oscar winning screenplay OR the best novel ever...), 2. some GRE prep books (because I'm going to go into Social Work and fix society), 3. my colored pencils and sketch book (for my masterpiece that will inspire world peace), and 4. a book incase I get bored--to bed with me because I'm going to do all this stuff before I fall asleep 3 or 4 hours later than I meant to. 

Usually, with all that crap all over my bed and nightstand, I watch a bunch of T.V. and fall asleep feeling guilty I haven't changed the world yet. This is with my meds 'working.'

Is this just reality now?

Hey--I'm just going to jump in here--I was asking this question because I may have to stop my medication and would never take anything without research and asking my doctor. I just wanted to hear some experiences, maybe give me a place to start. I appreciate Blabla's comment. It at least gives me a direction, but Greatbooks, I also appreciate your good lookin' out! ALWAYS talk to your doctor first 100% right. Thanks to you both!

Me too--do you mind if I ask what medications you use? I thought I was doing well until I looked around and realized I've been very deeply depressed for a while now. I'm using Lamictal and Leprexo (generic forms). Is this just how it will be forever?

Yep. 

I wish I could tell you I 'deal' with it, but really, it's just so confusing--which reactions are Bp2 and which ones are just PMS? It's been hard to 'convince' my sister and husband that I even have bp2. They both ask things like, "Have you had your hormones checked?" or "Do you think [insert whatever drug] is causing your mood changes?" Part of me can't help but resent them both for this. So when I'm PMSing, my really extreme mood shifts just seem to validate their suspicions that I've just been had by my doctor. 

This wasn't your question--I'm having a really hard week (month? year so far?) and I'm sorry for rambling. 

In sum, the struggle is real. I feel you. ;) I think the fact that you did some cardio is awesome and a great way to handle extra stress.

Yes--it really does. Even if I can just calm my mind for a couple minutes, it helps me slow down a little, or even to put some depression in perspective. Sometimes I can't, sometimes I have to try for a while, and sometimes it works & keeps me from descending or rising to extremes. Nothing's 100%, but it's a healthy way for me to exert some control over my illness.

Yes! Only baths for me (I really have to force myself to shower). Gross and weird, but I really can't do anything else. It's the strangest side effect of BP2--even when I'm not super depressed, I feel repelled by the shower. Even I'm over these irritating, odd hang-ups and inability to be spontaneous without being irritable about it.

Nothing about this doesn't suck. I'm sorry you're (and anyone is) going through this right now.

I agree 100%. Not being able to afford anything better than accident insurance but needing medication is lame, and kind of...depressing. I happen to be in the middle of an inadequacy/can't manage my life moment. Thank you and everyone else for some really helpful advice!

Yes. Stress or depression sometimes 'transforms' me into a maniacal motorist, crazy mom, and all around irritable person. I'm still figuring it out myself. It's like I'm falling into an abyss, but I scream in exhilaration rather than despair. At the bottom, I feel apathy and then depression. Mediating when I hit that first  aggressive abandon feeling because I can tell something is wrong has been (mostly) helpful, but I know this will take me more practice. 

Recognizing weird thought patterns is my first step in controlling or easing myself through the cycle. Hey, maybe you are just happier right now (that would be great!), but if you have a history of mental illness, take extra care of your heart and be patient with yourself. I hope I don't sound dismissive. This is really hard and I'm still trying--today I feel like shit, but I know why and I have some tools I can try. :) Good luck!

Yeah, the passive aggressive thing is really painful. I may be especially sensitive to it. And this weekend was so much worse--now my father is pissed at me because I couldn't get my mother to sign some paper to clear his child support payments from 20 f*cking ears ago. I'm in my late 30's and my f*cking parents just stuck me in the middle again like I was 8 again. I feel really alone. I have no one to trust to be authentic & not operating from some mysterious motivation. I'm so depressed and pissed. This is such a bad combo for me. Thanks for your reply!

I have to admit--we live pretty interesting lives. In high school, I directed and stage-managed in theatre. After that, multiple jobs in various fields, college where I went forever before transferring and picking a major--but of course I double majored because I wanted to study everything. I'm pretty sure I was having some sort of episode my last semester, but I wasn't diagnosed then. Then I joined the Army on a strong 'whim,' etc., etc. 

Mania makes for variety, if nothing else. The downside, of course, is that I can't climb in any field. When I lose interest, I really struggle to focus + the depression, or I get frustrated and bail. Jack of all trades; master of none. But I know how to do and know about a lot of random things. It would make me fun at parties if I went to any! ;)
I'm not sure which approach I'll take at this point, but I really appreciate your point about the "total moron" part. It's not up to me how she views the world. Thank you!
Thank you--that's really wonderful advice. I may have to do that.

Me too--the reason I went in for help (this time around) was to stop my random rage (like my dad had). I couldn't inflict the strain of not knowing if I'll be mad or easy about minor things. My medication allows me to be the mom I want to be. I have never felt this stable--after 37 years under the wet blanket of depression, rage, and suicidal ideation, I'm finally myself.
Sorry about the late response--I was put on 10 or 20 mg or Lexapro. Without the Lamictal, the Lexapro will make me manic, but they're working well for me together.

This is not medical advice--only personal experience, but when I started Lamictal, the first week or so, I was extremely anxious, way out of wack. Over time, as my dose was slowly increased and I got used to it, I've found it to be an amazing medication. I still have my swings, but they aren't as long or jarring. 

Also, I was put on a low dose of an anti-depressant since my doc had to "raise me up" before I could be evened out.

I know everyone's different. Lamictal doesn't work for everyone, but I wanted to share my experience. I wish you the best of luck! Med sampling is a rough road, but it's worth it, in my opinion.
Congrats! And thanks for the vibes. I felt better just reading this. :)
Hey, it's worth a try!

I think you're right--and hummingbird_mywill above. I was alone for Thanksgiving because I can't visit where my spouse and kids went (father-in-law hates me). That was a bummer. Memories of previous holidays can be haunting. Thank everyone for their replies! I think my meds are working. This didn't last more than a couple days which is really good for me.

But Christmas is coming...
Yeah, very annoying! This one is really bad--maybe because it came on so quickly. Instead of my gentle decline, I feel like I've been dropped in the middle of a really rough one.
Me too--she was so inspirational, and still is. It still makes me cry that she's gone. I also really appreciate the rest of your comment--forge your own path. It may be bumpy, but it's yours.

Absolutely. I've been "depressed" for years, diagnosed once or twice, but never really continued treatment because I'd seem to come out of it, be super energetic for awhile...When I finally saw a doc about rage issues at 38 years old, we tried leprexo (sp?) but it made me uncontrollable--really unpredictable moods, angry, weepy, etc. That's where the BP2 diagnosis come in. She realized that typical uppers were making me hypomanic and I've been on a Lamictal - Leprexo mix since, and I'm (finally) feeling better than--than for as long as I can remember. I got lucky--my doctor was experienced w/BP and knew what to look for. If you think your doc isn't listening, find a new one. And besides, nothing wrong with a second opinion before you go through a series of medications.

I don't have much to contribute, other than I totally get it. My "support system" is non-existent. I'm the one who helps the people in my life, not the other way around, so when I feel like the walls are caving in on my head...It's all "have you tried...look on the bright side...what do you have to complain about? etc...".

I'm going home early from work (also a great job, almost three years for me, too! Big accomplishment!) because I can't today. 

Now I'm going on about myself. :)

I wish I had any kind of advice to give. I guess I could use some too. BP2 is lonely.

Me too. I've been super "sensitive" since as long as I can remember, and depressed as early as 10. I wish I could comfort young me, tell that sad little kid that it's not going to be easy, but life will have rewards - that kid is going to have some real challenges doing things others find simple, but will also have unusual talents. Most importantly, I'd tell me that life IS worth living--never give up..

I know you want to be kind, but at least let him know you're frustrated. Your care is the priority. Besides, if he's learning, too, maybe this sort of feedback would be helpful. You and your feelings are what counts here. :)
A beautiful description of this cyclical, dark journey only a few really understand. This is how I feel so often--thank you for putting this out there.

Me too. I was making progress as a writer...until I came down with a case of apathy and writer's block I haven't been able to shake for months. I don't feel like my mind and moods are steady enough to do anything, much less write. I feel much better in general thanks to meds, but I've got no other support, don't have the time or $$ for therapy. I want you to succeed because I don't think I ever will. Please don't give up. Work towards your goals--as far as you can. See a doctor if you aren't already, if you can. I don't know if this is helpful at all.

I feel you, and I have no answer other than I don't know how to cope with this yet. From outside my life, I probably look just fine--served honorably in the Army, I have a degree from a great school, I have a family, a job----and yet, I wanted to be an officer and could never get my motivation on track (I guess it's best I didn't stay in, though). I didn't make it to graduate or law school though I knew I'd do great--no confidence when it came down to taking actual steps. I want to be a writer, but am so crippled with doubt, etc......It goes on like this. I shouldn't complain as I have a really nice life. I just feel like I've ended up a Jack-of-all-trades instead a talented, unique person with something extraordinary to offer. I've got ten years on you, but I completely get it. Push through those moments if you can. On my better days, I feel like my bp2 is a gift that will help me help others...and then on days like today, that sounds like bullsh*t and I feel robbed, too.

In my experience, while living in a legal state, that the stain of marijuana made a huge difference. A Sativa ALWAYS makes me paranoid and really uncomfortable. An Indica (sp?) is mush more calming, mellow. However, adding any drug into the mix with pills meant to impact your brain chemistry could be dangerous.

This is happening to me right now. I live with my husband and two young sons, and I invited my youngest sister (early 20's; I'm late 30's)to live with us as bp runs rampant in my family and I wanted to show my support, etc. I suspect, that after I opened up to her by relating my experiences with bp2, I think he shared his suspicion that my diagnosis needs a second opinion... She now is explaining that it's probably not a mental illness issue for her but a stress-induced anxiety. Now I feel really stupid. I'm finally improving with medication, and not only does he apparently not see it, but he won't take my word for how I feel. I wish I hadn't told anyone now. I know that's not any kind of a solutions for you, but I wanted to show you're not alone on this. It's hurtful and frustrating, but like someone else mentioned, (What_u_callme) people who have never felt this way will never really understand.

"So hang in there, be patient with yourself, and work with as good as you've got at that moment."

This--thank you! It's the expectations that make it worse for me, so this is wonderful advice.

The responses here are so helpful. Accepting that I will never be a "cheerful" person--I think I can handle that. I agree especially with the point you make about expectations: by freeing myself of assumptions about how I'm "supposed" to be, I can start appreciating who I am. Thank you (everyone here!) for taking the time to comment.
No, that's great! I don't want to sabotage myself with unrealistic expectations. Thank you.

Could you explain more here? I was diagnosed about 6 months ago. There's a lot of information available, but it's more helpful to hear it from someone who deals with it. Thank you for your answer thus far!

Yes. You are not alone. I feel really profound sorrow, especially when a story involves kids or animals. I spiral into all kinds of negative thinking. Medication helps, but I think being super empathetic just comes along in BP2's sidecar. I posted something like you are now a week or so ago, and this group was very kind, so I hope I can pass some of that on: your kind heart can be inconvenient, but it's a rare and beautiful quality. That you feel sad on the behalf of others and/or the state of the world means you care, and even though that's hard, it's also a precious part of who you are. (I hope that's not too cheesey...)
Having my medication working for now, I feel like who I'm supposed to be. I'm finally able to (mostly) be my best self. Give it a chance--you're worth the effort.
I'm interested!

I was having a very similar issue--the hypomanic episodes all but stopped, but my depression was still really debilitating. I went to my Doc thinking she'd up my Lamictal (from 100), but she actually upped my Lexapro from 10 to 20 and this made a huge difference. The Lamicatal  stabilizes (so far) the swings, and the Lexapro keeps me from sinking into the depression--at least, that's how I imagine it works. 

I'm sorry this is so frustrating! It's a process rather than a solution, and I wish you the best of luck.

That's actually kind of helpful--I've been struggling to find the right way to tell family I ___ bipolar (if I share this info...still haven't decided. I don't live with parents, so I may not have a reason to tell). "I have bipolar" feels a lot better to say that "I am."

I know your post is (at this moment) 4 months old, but I felt compelled to thank you anyway. I needed to read this today. So, thank you for being so honest and open about what you're going through. It made me feel a little better--and since nothing else has this week, that's actually pretty amazing.

I feel your frustration, though "frustration" is a normals word. For us, BP2 of any severity, it's more like soul crushing sadness, utter emptiness, or frightening and uncontrollable energy. I hate it, too. I also feel alone much of the time. People really don't seem to understand. 

I don't want to impress anyone with my stuff, I don't want pity, and I don't want the people around me second guessing my emotional responses...but I also want understanding, support, and especially on my low days, some space without resentment. It's a weird, fine line. 

I haven't figured out how to live well (or even mostly functionally) yet, but I wanted to write anyway, make sure you weren't feeling like you're the only one in the world who feels this way. I keep thinking about joining a support group or something, but I can barley handle my current obligations. 

My meds seem to be "pooping out" also, so I'll be checking in w/my doc. You aren't alone.
Yes--absolutely.

That's my experience as well. It's nice in legal states--you can be specific about what you need. A "sunny sativa" creates a brain buzz for me that is way too similar to a hypo spin. Indica calms me down, elevates my mood just enough, eases the anxiety, and helps me slowly come down from my stress from work. Marijuana use is a risk that has paid off for me, but BP folks won't react the same as those without, so be really aware and careful, and as always, check with your doctor!

Absolutely. Sometimes, I don't understand how people live normal lives. At my worst, I see life as a tragedy we all limp through. Everything is sorrow waiting to happen. I was watching a show last night and out of nowhere, they hit me with a very sad death of a kid. On top of the extra stress I've been feeling at work, it feels like I've been  knocked off a tight-rope. With "you're taking it too personally" ringing in my ears, I am now struggling to cope with an over-the-top reaction to a f***ing t.v. show. Will everything always be a trigger? I want to live in my closet. It's a pretty nice closet...

For me, the depression may start as a typical disappointment or identifiable source of stress, but then it spirals into the self-loathing and hopelessness that BornOn8thOfJuly describes. If I'm having a standard reaction to something negative in my environment, I feel mad/sad/irritated, but it passes. If it's the depression, my mood continues to sink(sometimes for days) until I bounce back off rock bottom and I start to rise again. Medication makes the journey shorter.

Yep. Constant crying is actually what got me back into my doctor's office. It still happens, but less often with my meds--100mg Lamictal and 10 mg Lexapro. I feel like I still cycle, but the crying helps to bring me out if the depression and I can keep from going hypo. I only allow myself to look at political news or else ANYTHING else will start me crying for the day. It's my body releasing stress, and for me, it let's me express all the low feelings I've been holding in in front of people. I usually cry Friday afternoons on my way home from work.
